# Postmortem: Checkout API outage, connection pool exhaustion

*Illustrative values in [brackets]. Replace with real data before publishing.*

**Date:** [YYYY-MM-DD] | **Duration:** 4h 0m ([HH:MM]-[HH:MM] UTC) | **Severity:** SEV-1
**Author:** [name] | **Status:** Draft | **Format:** blameless

## Summary

A slowdown in [downstream service, e.g. the pricing service] raised p99 latency from ~[80 ms] to ~[30 s]. Our API held DB/HTTP connections for the full duration of each downstream call, so the pool ([N] connections per instance) filled. New requests queued, timed out, and returned 5xx. Health checks shared the same pool, so instances were marked unhealthy and restarted, which dropped warm connections and made recovery slower. ~[X]% of requests failed for 4 hours.

## Impact

- [X]% of requests failed (5xx/timeouts) at peak; [Y] users affected.
- [Z] failed transactions, est. revenue impact [$].
- [N] support tickets; SLA/SLO budget for [month] fully consumed.

## Timeline (UTC)

| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| [10:02] | Downstream begins degrading after [deploy/config change/traffic spike]. Not alerted: no latency alert on that dependency. |
| [10:09] | Pool utilization hits 100% on first instances. Request queueing starts. |
| [10:14] | Error-rate alert fires (5xx > [5]%). On-call paged. |
| [10:25] | On-call acknowledges. Suspects own service; checks recent deploys, finds none. |
| [10:40] | Restarts instances. Brief recovery (~2 min), then pool refills. Misdiagnosis reinforced as "bad instance state". |
| [11:15] | Scales out API 2x. No improvement: each new instance exhausts its pool too, and load on downstream rises. |
| [11:50] | Pool metrics and thread dumps show all connections waiting on downstream calls. Downstream identified as the cause. |
| [12:10] | Downstream team engaged; reports they are degraded from [cause]. |
| [12:45] | Mitigation attempted: raise pool size. Worsens it by adding load on the already slow downstream. Reverted. |
| [13:20] | Downstream timeout lowered from [60 s] to [2 s] via config; circuit breaker flag enabled. |
| [13:50] | Error rate falling. Fallback (cached/default response) serving degraded results. |
| [14:02] | Error rate < 0.1%. Downstream recovers separately at [14:30]. Incident resolved. |

## Root cause

Three things combined:

1. **No bounded wait on the dependency.** The client timeout was [60 s] (effectively the library default), far above normal latency. One slow dependency could hold every pool slot.
2. **No isolation.** Request handlers, health checks, and non-dependent endpoints shared one pool. A failure in one dependency took down unrelated functionality.
3. **No load shedding or circuit breaking.** Retries ([3x]) multiplied traffic to the struggling downstream, and queued requests waited long past client timeouts, doing work nobody was waiting for.

Little Law makes this predictable: in-flight = arrival rate × latency. At [500 rps] and 30 s latency, [15,000] in-flight requests against a pool of [N].

## Contributing factors

- No alert on downstream latency; detection only came from our own 5xx rate.
- Dashboards lacked pool utilization and wait time.
- Runbook had "restart and scale out" as first steps, which don't help here and increase downstream load.
- Diagnosis took ~90 min to point outward because no dependency-level latency metrics existed.

## What went well

- Error-rate alert paged within 12 minutes of the first impact.
- Timeout and circuit-breaker flags could be changed at runtime without a deploy.
- Downstream team responded within 20 minutes of being engaged.

## What went poorly

- Time to identify cause (~110 min).
- Pool-size increase made things worse.
- Restarts discarded warm state and caused brief flapping.

## Remediation

| # | Action | Type | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Set per-call timeouts on all dependencies (p99 × ~3, max [2 s] here) | Prevent | [name] | [date] |
| 2 | Circuit breaker with fallback on [downstream] and other critical dependencies | Prevent | [name] | [date] |
| 3 | Bulkheads: separate pools/concurrency limits per dependency; dedicated pool for health checks | Prevent | [name] | [date] |
| 4 | Retry policy: max 1 retry, jittered backoff, retry budget (~10% of traffic) | Prevent | [name] | [date] |
| 5 | Load shedding: cap queue wait; reject fast with 503 + `Retry-After` when pool wait > [500 ms] | Mitigate | [name] | [date] |
| 6 | Alerts: dependency p99 latency, pool utilization > 80%, pool wait time | Detect | [name] | [date] |
| 7 | Dashboard: per-dependency latency, error rate, in-flight, pool wait | Detect | [name] | [date] |
| 8 | Runbook: "pool exhausted" playbook (check dependency latency first; lower timeouts; don't raise pool size or blindly scale out) | Respond | [name] | [date] |
| 9 | Game day: inject [5 s] latency into each critical dependency in staging; verify breaker and shedding | Verify | [name] | [date] |
| 10 | Agree latency SLOs and timeout budgets with downstream owners | Process | [name] | [date] |

## Lessons

- A dependency being slow is worse than it being down: failures return fast, slowness holds resources.
- Timeouts are a capacity setting, not just an error-handling setting.
- Adding capacity (pool, instances) on the caller side amplifies load on a struggling dependency.

## Open questions

- Why did downstream degrade at [10:02]? Pending their postmortem: [link].
- Are other services using the same default timeout? Audit under action #1.
